text: The 1958 French presidential election was the first held under the French Fifth Republic, taking place on 21 December. It was the only presidential election conducted by an electoral college composed of members of the French Parliament, general councils, overseas assemblies, and tens of thousands of mayors, deputy mayors, and municipal councillors. To win, a candidate needed over 50% of the vote, a system that was later abolished following a 1962 referendum. Charles de Gaulle, who became President of the Council of Ministers (Prime Minister) after the May 1958 crisis amid the Algerian War, won a landslide victory in the first round with 78.5% of the votes cast, defeating Georges Marrane of the French Communist Party (PCF) and Albert Châtelet of the Union of Democratic Forces (UFD). De Gaulle took office on 8 January 1959, and after the 1962 referendum, he established direct universal suffrage for presidential elections, beginning in 1965, which led to his re-election. The election occurred during the Algerian War and after the May 1958 crisis, when, on 1 June 1958, de Gaulle, previously President of the Provisional Government of the French Republic, was appointed Prime Minister at the request of President René Coty. Three months later, on 30 September 1958, the Constitution of the Fifth Republic was adopted by referendum with 82.6% of "yes" votes. The return of de Gaulle to power, including his investiture by the National Assembly amid high tension, was denounced by the left, particularly the PCF, which viewed it as a "coup d'état." The Radical Party and the French Section of the Workers' International (SFIO) joined his government, with Guy Mollet as Minister of State, but opposition within these parties led to schisms, resulting in the formation of the UFD, which included figures such as Pierre Mendès France and François Mitterrand (UDSR). The election took place during the Cold War, and the PCF, the dominant party after the Second World War, feared that public opinion was turning against the Eastern Bloc and the USSR. The legislative elections of November 1958 saw a Gaullist right victory and a historic decline in left-wing deputies, with only 10 communists elected—down from 150 in 1956—while the UFD secured less than 2% of the votes and no seats. Article 6 of the 1958 Constitution states that the President is elected for seven years by an electoral college including members of Parliament, general councils, overseas assemblies, and elected representatives of municipal councils, with the latter varying by commune size. Article 7 retains the two-round majority single-member constituency system. Due to the large number of sparsely populated communes, the electoral college favors rural areas, often referred to as "France du seigle et de la châtaigne" (France of rye and chestnuts), as communes with fewer than 4,000 inhabitants have three times more delegates than those with over 100,000 inhabitants. The November 7, 1958 organic law outlines voting procedures, requiring candidates to collect at least 12 signatures from the electoral college at least 12 days before the first round, with electors voting in their departmental capital. If no candidate achieves a majority, a second round is held within eight days. The decision to avoid direct universal suffrage resulted from a compromise with de Gaulle’s opponents, who feared a break with the Fourth Republic, and because the French colonial Empire was expected to vote overwhelmingly for de Gaulle, which would have given him a decisive advantage under direct suffrage. On 13 December 1958, the Provisional Constitutional Commission announced that Albert Châtelet, honorary dean of the Paris Faculty of Sciences, had gathered the required signatures to run, a candidacy initiated by Daniel Mayer and supported by the UFD, which stated it opposed the "dangerous simplification" of French politics as a battle between two blocs. During the campaign, de Gaulle, at 70 years old, was seen as the clear favorite due to his prestige and position, and the electoral system, resulting in a lack of intense or media-heavy campaigning. Châtelet, who believed de Gaulle and the communists contained the seeds of civil war, refused to campaign, calling his candidacy "symbolic and principled." As predicted, de Gaulle secured an absolute majority without needing a second round. In Metropolitan France alone (excluding Algeria and overseas territories), 74,391 votes were cast: 77.5% for de Gaulle, 13.6% for Georges Marrane, and 8.9% for Albert Châtelet. Although de Gaulle won all departments, his opponents did not consider the victory humiliating. Marrane achieved his best results in communist strongholds, particularly in Nord-Pas-de-Calais, while Châtelet came second in 39 metropolitan departments, notably in socialist and radical areas in southern France.
